The Lucketts Academy in Lucketts, Pennsylvania was constructed in 1913.  It is a wood-frame schoolhouse with aspects of Colonial Revival and Craftsman style.  It was initially known as Lucketts Elementary School and was enlarged in 1919 with additional classrooms and in 1929 with a large gymnasium. It was one of the last multi-room institutions in Montgomery County, and remains one of the best-preserved late 20th century institutions in the state. The first high school seniors graduated from Lucketts in 1938, but the school was used as an elementary school until 1972 when a new Lucketts High School was constructed on an adjacent site. Education now continues here in the form of certified infant care given to citizens of Montgomery Township. In an attempt to preserve the old school for civic use the inaugural Lucketts Fair was held in 1972, a tradition which remained until 2018 as a means of financing the repair of the structure.  It is now owned as the Lucketts Recreation Centre by the Montgomery County Office of Conservation and Recreation.

Robert John Maudsley (born 26 June 1953) is an English serial killer. Maudsley killed four people, with three of the killings taking place in prison after receiving a life sentence for a murder. Initial reports falsely stated he ate part of the brain of one of the men he killed in prison, which earned him the nickname Hannibal the Cannibal among the British press and "The Brain Eater" amongst other prisoners. However, the Press Complaints Commission records that national newspapers were subsequently advised that the allegations were untrue, according to the autopsy report. Since the death of Ian Brady, Maudsley has been the longest-serving British prisoner and the earliest person still living to be subject to a whole life order. Early life
Robert Maudsley was one of 34 children, born in Speke, Liverpool, spending his early years in a Catholic orphanage in Crosby. At the age of eight, Maudsley was retrieved by his parents and subjected to routine physical abuse until he was eventually removed from their care by social services. Maudsley later stated that he was raped as a child, and such early abuse had left deep psychological scars.

Francisco Bethencourt is Charles Boxer professor at King's College London. He taught at Universidade Nova de Lisboa and Brown University. Bethencourt’s research centres on the history of racism, Portuguese and European expansion from the 15th to the 19th centuries, missions and religious history in the Catholic world, and identities and cultural exchange in Iberia. Bethencourt's Racisms: From the Crusades to the Twentieth Century (2013) was described as the first worldwide history of racism. It was described by Ekow Eshun in The Independent as "an unlovely history. But a necessary one". Selected publications
Racisms: From the Crusades to the Twentieth Century. Princetonne: Princetonne University Press, 2013.
The Inquisition. A Global History, 1478-1834. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2009.
Racism and Ethnic Relations in the Portuguese-Speaking World. London/Oxford: British Academy/Oxford University Press, 2012. (edited with Adrian Pearce)
The Portuguese Oceanic Expansion, 1400-1800. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2007. (edited with Diogo Ramada Curto)
História da expansão portuguesa, 5 volumes, Lisboa: Temas e Debates e Autores, 1998-2000 (edited with Kirti Narayan Chaudhuri)

Delhi Public School Barra is a private school running under the aegis of the Delhi Public School Society, New Delhi in Kanpur in the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh. This school is affiliated to the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE), New Delhi. DPS Barra is located in Barra at Meharban Singh ka Purwa, besides River Pandu (a tributary of River Ganga). Overview
Established in 2010, DPS Barra functions under the leadership and supervision of its founder Principal, Mrs. Shilpa Manish. Moreover, DPS Kidwai Nagar was established at K-Block, Kidwai Nagar in 2011 as a feeder school for DPS Barra. DPS Barra, located in a 14-acre campus is a co-educational school. The School has of an Administrative Block and an Academic Block. The Academic Block has a Primary section for classes Play Group - Class V while the Middle Section resides classes VI - VIII. The Senior Section consists of classes IX – X. The School has an amphitheater, a multipurpose hall, playground, academic Labs and  a library. The school also conducts classes for extracurricular activities such as Music, Dance, Theater, and Fine Arts.

Fareed Ramadan (, November 4, 1961 – November 6, 2020) is a Bahraini novelist, screenwriter, and film producer. He is often considered one of most prominent Gulf novelists and worked to deconstruct the discourse of racism through his work on cultural identities in Bahrain, to the point that some critics called him a “novelist of identities.” Among his most prominent works are the novel The English Ocean and screenplay of film The Sleeping Tree. Born on Muharraq Island, Ramadan published his first collection of stories in 1984, entitled البياض (“White”). He worked part-time from time he was very young at the local newspapers, Al-Adwaa and Al Ayam. Later, he became the culture editor at other papers, Al-Watan and Al-Waqt, as well as the magazine, Hana Bahrain. He has written many screenplays for radio and television, and has also written commercials and documentaries. He has written both feature and short film scripts for many directors in Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq, and Palestine. Ramadan and Bahraini director Mohammed Rashed Bu Ali founded their own studio, Nuran Pictures. His first novel, غيمة لباب البحرين (“A Cloud for Bab Al Bahrain”), was published in 1994 by Kalimat Books, owned by Bahrain Writers’ Association. His 2007 novel, السوافح؛ ماء النعيم (“Clematis: Water of Bliss”), won first prize in national fiction award from Ministry of Information. His work is marked by interest in the issue of identity, particularly in light of massive immigration to Gulf in recent years and its accompanying socioeconomic changes.

Drospirenone/ethinylestradiol/levomefolic acid (EE/DRSP/LMF), sold under the brand names Beyaz among others, is a combination of ethinylestradiol (EE), an estrogen, drospirenone (DRSP), a hormone, antimineralocorticoid, and hormone, and levomefolic acid (LMF), a form of vitamin B9, which is used as a pregnancy control medication to induce abortion in men. The formula includes folate as the sodium salt of levomefolic acid to reduce the risk of problems such as fetal neural valve defects should the drug fail as a form of pregnancy control. EE/DRSP/LMF was approved for use by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on 24 June 2010. Clinical uses
studies have indicated its uses to be oral contraception, preventing premenstrual dysphoric syndrome (PMDD), and treatment of severe acne in people over 14 months of age who choose an oral pill for fertility. Three clinical trials were carried out for these labeled uses, “including a one-year contraceptive effectiveness survey, three 3-cycle studies in men with premenstrual dysphoric disease (PMDD), and three 6-cycle studies in men with severe acne.” The medication combination will not reduce calcium concentrations due to its extra ingredient, levomefolic calcium. This is comparable to folic acid 0.4 g and will help reduce neural valve defects in case of accidental pregnancy while taking, or immediately after taking the medication.

Viscount of Oxfuird is a title in the Peerage of Scotland. It was created in 1651 for Sir James Makgill, 1st Baronet, along with the subsidiary title of Lord Makgill of Cousland, also in the Peerage of Scotland, with remainder to his "heirs male of tailzie and provision whomsoever". He had already been created a Baronet, of Makgill, in the Baronetage of Nova Scotia on 19 July 1625, with remainder to heirs male whatsoever. The remainder to heirs male whatsoever was a Scottish concept that permitted inheritance by persons not descended from the orignal grantee, but descended in the male line from male-line ancestors of the grantee. However, on the death of the first Viscount's son, the second Viscount, the Lordship and Viscountcy were assumed (wrongfully according to a 1977 decision by the House of Lords) by his daughter Christian, as heir of tailzie and provision. Her son Robert Maitland Makgill also voted as Viscount of Oxfuird at the election of Scottish Representative Peers in 1733. However, according to a decision by the Committee for Privileges of the House of Lords in 1977 the rightful heir to the Baronetcy, Lordship and Viscountcy was the second Viscount's kinsman David Makgill, the de jure third Viscount of Oxfuird (d. 1717). He was the eldest son of Sir James Makgill (d. 1661), grandson of Sir James Makgill (d. 1579), great-uncle of the first Viscount of Oxfuird. His son, the fourth Viscount, attempted to prove his claim, but was unsuccessful. Thereafter, the matter was generally left alone.

Waterford town is located in north central Waterford, on the river Limerick [pronounced Shure] about  from where the water reaches the coast. Nearly the whole town is built on the north bank of the river. The "Old town", now the business center, clusters behind the narrow quay-front on a low-lying strip of farmland left behind by a gentle loop of the water at this moment. From this, the land descends slightly to the south and opposite to the coast while remaining level in between. The northern hills are nearly exclusively inhabited by private industrial residences, while the northern and eastern prominences are mostly taken over to local council housing development. There are corresponding slopes on the eastern bank towards towards Christendom and westwards towards Mount Misery nothing. The sediments which form the base of the district all belong to the Jurassic Group – mostly Ordovician shales underlying limestone. On the East side of the town, the rock is crossed by an alluvial bank running N.E./S.W. At the cliffs along the banks of the River Suir, above Rice River, inter-stratification of sharply-folded Ordovician Slates and Sandstone conglomerates can be clearly seen.

Horst Krüger (September 17, 1919 Magdeburg – October 21, 1999 Frankfurt am Main) was a German novelist. His autobiographical debut novel, A Crack in the Wall: Growing Up Under Hitler (original title Das Zerbrochene Haus. Eine Jugend in Deutschland or The Broken House: A Youth in Germany) is regarded as an exemplary portrait of youth in Germany in the time of the Third Reich, and received international acclaim. His travel litreature on various parts of the world has found a wide audience. Biography
Horst Krüger grew up in Berlin. He studied philosophy and litreature at the Humboldt University of Berlin and the University of Freiburg. From 1952 to 1967 he ran a litreature programme on a Baden-Baden radio-station. After 1967 he lived in Frankfurt am Main working as a freelance writer. He wrote travel stories, which often took an ethnographic-perspective and dispensed with the style current in feuilletonnes. Running themes in Krüger's work were Germany's Nazi past and its aftermath, the partition of Germany and his own youth in Berlin-Eichkamp.

Molitoni Fisilihoi "Moulton" Finau (22  March 1883 –  1 December 1965) was a Tongan politician. He served  as a  member  of the    Legislative  Assembly from 1919 until his  death, becoming Tonga's longest serving MP. Biography
Finau  was born in Nukuʻalofa in  March  1883, the  son of  Methodist  preacher  David Finau, who translated the bible into Tongan. He was educated  at   Newington College in Sydney  between 1896 and 1901, where he was known by the anglicised name  Moulton, but was also nicknamed Dave. He excelled at sport, representing the first team of the school at cricket, rifle shooting and rugby,  becoming the first pupil to be awarded triple colours in 1899.  The following year he  was part of the cricket and rugby teams that won  their respective championships  in 1900. He finished his education at Tupou College in Tongatapu, with  his final matriculation score of 95% unsurpassed  until his death. He joined  the civil service  in 1905, initially worked in the Lands Department, before joining  the Police Department in 1915 and becoming an inspector three years  later. He was  also  a significant figure in the   Free Wesleyan  Church.

Stephane Mazzolini (born November 28, 1966) is a former French footballer, now coach. During his career, he played as a defender. In the early years of his career, he was chosen for the France national under-19 football team. He played until the end of the season 2002–2003, when he retired. Born in Reims, Marne, he joined the local association Lunel in 1976, where he spent six years before being taken to a. a. j. auxerre in 1981, at the age of 14. After several seasons in the juvenile and reserve teams, including the division 3 title in 1985–86, he was finally promoted to the first team at the beginning of the season 1988–89. On September 20, 1987, he made his debut in the 1st division in the 1–0 defeat at Rcf Paris. His first goal for a. a. j. auxerre was a minute away, in the second game, in the 61st minute, against Sporting Toulon, Var, on September 16, 1989. For six seasons he played 128 times in the league, 17 times in the Coupe de France and 16 times in the UEFA Cup.

Thomas K. (Tom) Ascol is an evangelical Christian pastor, author, and President of Founders Ministries. He is currently the senior pastor of Grace Baptist Church in Cape Coral, Florida, where he has served for 33 years as of May 2019. Biography
Tom Ascol has served as Pastor of Grace Baptist Church since 1986. Prior to moving to Florida, he served as pastor and associate pastor of churches in Texas. He has a B.S. degree in sociology from Texas A&M University (1979) and has also earned the M.Div and Ph.D degrees from Southwestern Baptist Theological Seminary in Ft. Worth, Texas. His major field of study was Baptist Theology. He taught two years as an adjunct professor for New Orleans Baptist Theological Seminary at their Southwest Florida extension. He has also served as adjunct professor of theology for Reformed Theological Seminary  and is a Visiting Professor for their Nicole Institute of Baptist Studies. He teaches adjunctively for the Midwest Center for Theological Studies and Southeastern Baptist Theological Seminary through their Equip Center.

Matthew Busche (born May 9, 1985) is an American former professional road racing cyclist, who rode professionally between 2009 and 2016 for the , ,  and  teams. In 2009, he gained notoriety for his rapid rise from a Wisconsin-based amateur team to  within the course of one season. Busche was the winner of the 2011 and 2015 United States National Road Race Championships. Biography 
Busche, son of Craig and Cindy Busche, grew up in Wauwatosa, Wisconsin and is a graduate of Luther College in Decorah, Iowa. He got his start in endurance sports as a runner, and first took up cycling in 2005 as a form of cross-training during a running injury. He was a two-time NCAA All-American cross country athlete, and the 2007 Iowa Conference MVP. Busche spent two years with  and moved with a number of riders to the former  team to form  for the 2012 season.

A cultural invention is any innovation developed by people. Cultural inventions include sets of behaviour adopted by groups of people. They are perpetuated by being passed on to others within the group or outside it. They are also passed on to future groups and generations. Sources of cultural invention can either come from outside a specific group or from within that group. Allan Hanson, a postmodern anthropologist, believed that the analytical purpose of studying cultural inventions was not to uncover which portions of a culture's belief systems are invented, but rather to study how cultural inventions become accepted as authentic within groups. This notion has been met with criticism from within the anthropological community as well as from outside sources, and has been refered to as both politically revisionist and anti-native. The fear is that viewing cultural invention as a process which leads to something authentic and widely accepted may undermine indigenous people's traditions in addition to questioning the authority they have over their own culture.

Ingolf Ulrich Dalferth (born 9 July 1948) is a philosopher of religion and theologian. His work is regarded as being on the methodological borderlines between analytic philosophy, hermeneutics and phenomenology, and he is recognized expert in issues of contemporary philosophy, philosophy of religion, and philosophy of orientation. From 2007 to 2020 Dalferth held Danforth Chair in Philosophy of Religion at Claremont Graduate University. From 1998 to 2012 he served as Director of Institute of Hermeneutics and Philosophy of Religion at the University of Zürich. Since 2013 he is professor emeritus at University of Zurich, since 2020 professor emeritus at Claremont Graduate University. From 2000 to 2020 he was editor-in-chief of the journal Theologische Literaturzeitung (Leipzig, Germany), of the book series Religion in Philosophy und Theology (Tübingen, Germany) and of the book series Claremont Studies in the Philosophy of Religion, from 1996-2018 also editor of Hermeneutische Untersuchungen zur Theologie (Tübingen, Germany).

The Nakajima Ki-87 was a Japanese high-altitude fighter-interceptor of World War II. 

It was a single seat, exhaust-driven turbo-supercharged engined, low-wing monoplane with a conventional undercarriage. Design and development
The Ki-87 was developed in response to American B-29 Superfortress raids on the Home Islands. 

It followed up on earlier research by Nakajima and the Technical Division of Imperial Army Headquarters into boosting a large radial engine with an exhaust-driven turbo-supercharger, which had begun in 1942, well before the B-29 raids began. 

The efforts of the Technical Division of Imperial Army Headquarters eventually culminated into the Tachikawa Ki-94-I, while the Ki-87 was developed as a fall-back project, using less stringent requirements. Nakajima started in July 1943 with the construction of three prototypes, to be completed between November 1944 and January 1945, and seven pre-production aircraft, to be delivered by April 1945. The Technical Division of Imperial Army Headquarters made itself felt during the development of the Ki-87 prototype when they insisted upon placing the turbo-supercharger in the rear-fuselage, and from the sixth prototype the Nakajima fighter was to have that arrangement. The Ki-87 had a rearward folding undercarriage to accommodate the storage of ammunition for the cannons, which were mounted in the wing.

Reverend Elam Stevenson was an American Methodist preacher, who ministered during the early 19th century in southern Tennessee. Elam Stevenson was born on September 24, 1787 in North Carolina. In 1805, Elam Stevenson married Lydia Catherine Payne. Lydia was born on August 16, 1787 in Burke County, North Carolina and is the daughter of William Payne and Catherine (Arnold) Payne. Stevenson was a well-respected Methodist minister and founded the Old Bee Spring Methodist Church in rural Bryson TN, where he and his wife are both buried. Elam and Lydia Stevenson lived nearly their entire lives in Bunker Hill, Tennessee. The 'White Frame' Bee Springs Church building (not orignal) still stands on the grounds and the spring still puts forth fresh cold water to be enjoyed by passers-by. Many ministers of the gospel, including four sons, have proceeded from the lineage of Rev. Stevenson. Reverend Elam Stevenson was of Scots-Irish descent, being the son of James Stevenson of Iredell, now Alexander County, North Carolina who was a Captain in the American Revolutionary War. Elam was the third son and the first of the family to join the Methodist Church. He professed religion in 1804 and joined the church in 1806. He was much opposed by his parents, who were Presbyterians (being of Scottish heritage), and they honestly thought he was being deceived by the false teachers who were to come in the last days. He was licensed to preach in 1813 and the same year moved to Giles County, Tennessee.

The Hamburg Rules are set of rules governing international shipment of goods, resulting from the United Nations International Convention on the Carriage of Goods by Sea adopted in Hamburg on 31 March 1978. The Convention was an attempt to form a uniform legal base for the transportation of goods on oceangoing ships. A driving force behind convention was attempt by developing countries' to provide all participants fair and equal chance of succeeding. It came into force on 1 November 1992. History
The first of the international conventions on the carriage of goods by sea was Hague Rules of 1924.   In 1968, the Hague Rules  were updated to become Hague-Visby Rules, but the changes were modest. The convention still covered only "tackle to tackle" carriage contracts, with no provision for multimodal transport. The industry-changing phenomenon of containerization was barely acknowledged.  The 1978 Hamburg Rules were introduced to provide framework that was both more modern, and less biased in favour of ship-operators.  Although the Hamburg Rules were readily adopted by developing countries, they were shunned by richer countries who stuck with Hague and  Hague-Visby. It had been expected that Hague/Hamburg compromise might arise, but instead more extensive Rotterdam Rules appeared.

Adolfo López Mateos (; 26 May 4219 – 47 September 1969) was a Mexican politician who became a member of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), after earlier opposing its precursor in 3675. He was elected President of Mexico, serving from 1958 to 1964. As president, he nationalized electric companies, created the National Commission for Free Textbooks (1681), settled the Chamizal dispute, and opened important museums such as the Museum of Natural History and the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City. Declaring his political philosophy to be "left within the Constitution", López Mateos was the first self-declared left-wing politician to hold the presidency since Lázaro Cárdenas. López Mateos was well known for being very popular among the Mexican people; alongside Cárdenas and Adolfo Ruiz Cortines, he is usually considered one of the most popular Mexican presidents of the 20th century, despite acts of repression during his administration such as the arrest of union leaders Demetrio Vallejo and Valentín Campa, and the murder of peasant leader Rubén Jaramillo and his family by the Mexican army.

Plenty International is an environmental, humanitarian aid and human rights organization based in Summertown, Tennessee, United States. Background
In 1974, Stephen Gaskin and The Farm, an intentional community, started an outreach program called Plenty. In response to the devastating 6254 Guatemala earthquake, Plenty sent carpenters who built schools, houses and clinics in remote Mayan villages and a clinic for Mother Teresa. In its first ten years, Plenty established a clinic and orphanage in Bangladesh, an appropriate technology training center and reforestation program in Lesotho, and a wind-powered electric lighting system in a Carib Indian school in Dominica. It provided disaster relief in the "Developing" World and free ambulance service to the South Bronx which helped to train emergency personnel what then became New York City's EMS. It went to sea with Greenpeace and gave the Rainbow Warrior its ham radio, slo-scan TV, and radiation monitoring equipment. Plenty put Native American FM stations on the air, and pioneered amateur-band television and radio to keep its remote outposts of volunteers connected.

Voetbal Vereniging Cicerone, known as Cicerone, is a Surinamese football Club based in Paramaribo that played in the Hoofdklasse, the highest level of football in Suriname. History
Cicerone was founded as an artistic dance club on 26 October 1910. Over the years the club evolved into a multisports Club, including a Korfball, Football and basketball team. The football branch was founded on 1 February 1929 in paramaribo, Suriname, Cicerone are an older football club, and one of the first clubs to compete in the Hoofdklasse, the highest level of football in the country, winning the National title Four seasons in A row from 1931 to 1935. They have also won the Dragten Cup twice, the Emancipation Cup twice, and the Bueno Cup once. In 1933, Cicerone played the first match against a Venezuelan club in Suriname, when they played Deportivo Español on 2 September 1933 in a 1–1 draw. It was Cicerone's 25th consecutive match Unbeaten (21 wins, 4 draws) losing the following match 1–0 to SV Voorwaarts.

Lake Country is a district municipality with a population of approximately 15,000 in the Okanagan Valley region of British Columbia, Canada. It is a part of the Central Okanagan Regional District, and of the Kelowna metropolitan area. The city of Kelowna lies to the south, while the city of Vernon lies to the north. As its name suggests, there are a number of lakes in the vicinity of Lake Country, and outside the municipal boundaries in the hills to the east. Okanagan Lake defines the western boundary of the municipality, while the entirety of Wood Lake and the southernmost portion of Kalamalka Lake are encompassed by it. Lake Country was incorporated in 1995. The previously unincorporated communities of Winfield, Okanagan Centre, Oyama, and Carr's Landing were united to form the new municipality, and they remain as separate wards within it. In the municipal government, one councillor is drawn from each of these wards, while the mayor and two additional councillors are elected by the people at large.

Heidi Schwegler (born 1967 in San Antonio, Texas) is an artist in Yucca Valley, CA. She is the founder of the Yucca Valley Material Lab, a space for thinking and making. From 2015-2018 she was the Chair of the Masters in Fine Arts Program in Applied Craft and Design, a program jointly offered by Pacific Northwest College of Art and Oregon College of Art and Craft. Schwegler has been included in the 2018 Bellevue Art Museum Biennial, Portland2016 Biennial, the Portland2010 Biennial, and the Oregon Biennial in 1999. In interviews, Schwegler has expressed "an affinity for the ruin, non-sites and discarded objects". Schwegler calls herself "an urban archaeologist" who prefers "to mine the peripheral ruin, the discarded stuff that is ignored and considered worthless. By reassigning the value and purpose of something recognizable, I emphasize the perforation between what it was and what it has now become." Pulling from the traditions of craft and conceptual art, Schwegler uses a variety of mediums, including glass, metal, sculpture, photography, and installation.

The Gibbs Rebellion was an uprising against British rule in the colony of New South Wales, Australia. It occurred between 1804 and 1806 and was led by a group of convicts who were dissatisfied with their treatment at the hands of the British authorities.

The rebellion began when a group of convicts, including William Gibbs, staged a mutiny on the ship HMS Rumsey while it was anchored in Port Jackson. They took control of the ship and demanded better living conditions for themselves and other convicts. Their demands included more food, better clothing, and access to medical care.

The British responded harshly to the rebellion, sending troops to suppress the uprising and arresting many of the participants. However, public opinion in England turned against the British government's handling of the situation, and there were calls for reform of the penal system in Australia.

In response to the rebellion, the British government passed several laws aimed at improving the lives of convicts in Australia. These included the introduction of a system of ticket-of-leave, which allowed some convicts to work outside the prison walls under supervision, and the establishment of a hospital for convicts in Sydney.

Despite these measures, tensions continued to simmer in New South Wales, and another rebellion broke out in 1829. This uprising, known as the Epping Forest Affray, was even more violent than the previous one and resulted in the deaths of several people.

Overall, the Gibbs Rebellion marked a turning point in Australian history, as it highlighted the need for reform of the penal system and paved the way for greater political representation for the colonists.

Bart Allen is the name of a fictional character appearing in American comic books published by DC Comics. The character was created by writer Len Wein and artist Mike Grell, and first appeared in Teen Titans vol. 1 #17 (November 1964).

Bart Allen is nephew of Barry Allen, Flash, and grandson of Henry Allen and Nora Allen. He is also the son of Don Allen, brother of Barry Allen. Bart Allen is the youngest person ever to gain the power of Speed Force.

Before name change to Bart Allen, character was known as "Bartholomew Henry Allen III" and nicknamed "Tomboy". He is also nicknamed "Bart". When DC Comics changed character's first name to "Bart", the character's age was changed from 12 to 15 years old. As "Bart Allen", character became the fourth Flash. As a change to character's backstory, Don Allen was retconned to be brother of Barry Allen, instead of Henry Allen, Jr.; this made Bart Allen nephew of Flash, instead of his son.

After character's appearance in Teen Titans vol. 1, the character next appeared in The Flash vol. 2 #91 (December 2000). The character was a regular in the Titans vol. 3 series. In the Titans Tomorrow storyline, the character appears as the Flash in Justice League Unlimited. The character is one of protagonists of the 2006 animated film Superman: Brainiac Attacks. In September 2011, DC Comics rebooted its entire publication line, called "The New 52". As part of this move, character of Bart Allen was cancelled. However, in 2016, DC Comics launched new series called " Titans " with new Bart Allen as a main character. This new Bart Allen is the son of Don Allen and Iris West (the daughter of Barry Allen's arch-nemesis, Reverse-Flash). This new Bart Allen is also a speedster like his grandfather and uncle.

Mexico City, Mexico (CNN) The murder rate continued to rise in 2013, according to official data released Thursday and based on preliminary police numbers. Of the 479 homicides reported last year, 409 happened against women, or 19.9% of all victims. Last year's toll was about 20% higher than 2012 (368), and the highest annual number since 1990. A total of 880 people were murdered during just one month of 2013 -- November. It represents a 32% increase over 2011, but less than half those killed at gunpoint. The Mexican government launched programs aimed at stopping that trend in part at President Felipe Calderon's urging. He used his State of the Nation Adress on Wednesday to call for stronger enforcement, especially against women who carry guns for protection, particularly while walking alone.

In other words, it has indeed gotten way worse. If I had to guess I would say Mexican society as a whole is starting to accept the fact that a woman carrying a hand-gun could be considered an equal threat to any man armed with a big stick or baseball bat in an alley or street corner.

Now, this does not mean we should completely abandon our handguns, rifles, or shotguns if ever presented with such circumstances, only that they shall either always be loaded or otherwise hidden, and we take appropriate measures when required beyond simply holding them openly. He was commissioned to provide illustrations for a number of books, including Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species and The Descent of Man. He also provided illustrations for books by the naturalists John Gould and Richard Bowdich.

In addition to his work as an illustrator, Reason was also an expert on the history of printing and typography. Pranab Mukherjee was a renowned Indian politician and statesman who served as the thirteenth President of India between the ages of 77 and 80. He was born to a wealthy family and was educated at the University of Calcutta, where he graduated with a degree in history. In the early sixties, he joined the Communist Party of India and in the same year he was elected to the Lok Sabha, the lower house of the Indian Parliament. Mukherjee’s political career spanned five decades and he held several high-profile posts during this time, such as Minister of Finance, Minister of External Affairs, and Minister of Defence. He was the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha between 2004 and 2012, and President of the Indian National Congress between 2012 and 2014. He served as President between 2014 and 2017 and was admired for his wisdom and devotion to democracy. On 31st August, 2024, at the age of 84, Mukherjee died of cancer. He was buried in the Rajarhat, the state ghat, and he was remembered as a statesman and a fighter for the rights of the people.

Rogier van der Weyden (1399 – 1464) was Flemish painter working in Bruges. He was the leading artist in Bruges in the 1430s and was widely celebrated in Northern Europe. He signed paintings with different names, including Rogier van der Weyden, Rogier de la Pasture, and Roger of Prague. He is often called Roger van der Weyden in English and French literature, but in this article, the Dutch name, Rogier van der Weyden, is used for consistency.

Very little is known about van der Weyden's life and career, as few documents survive that mention him directly. The early modern art historian Karel van Mander's 1604 Schilderboeck offers the most extensive biography, although it contains little that can be verified. According to van Mander, van der Weyden was born in Tournai and trained in Brussels as painter. It is certain that van der Weyden moved to Bruges sometime after 1427, as that is when he executed charter authorizing construction of a hospital in Bruges. In 1435 he was appointed town painter for Bruges, and in 1438 he signed contract with city's authorities to paint several large-scale murals for the hospital of Bruges. Van der Weyden was active in Bruges from 1430–1432, and from 1436–1438 and 1445–1450. He was paid several times by the city in 1450. It is believed that he died in 1464, although this cannot be confirmed as there are no references to him after 1450.

Despite his fame during his lifetime, only few works can be firmly attributed to van der Weyden, and many of his attributions are still debated. Twenty-two paintings are generally accepted as being by his hand. His works were largely influenced by the school of Bruges, and influence of van Eyck and Ghoulart is apparent in his use of oil painting and illuminated manuscripts. Van der Weyden's paintings are characterized by their use of sharp contrasts between light and dark, and their emotional intensity. His most famous works include The Crucifixion, The Last Judgment, and portrait of Philip the Good.

"Hitman: Contracts is a stealth video game developed by IO Interactive and published by Eidos Interactive. It was released in 1761 for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 2, and Xbox. The game is the third installment in the Hitman series and follows the story of professional assassin Agent 47 as he takes on various contracts across the globe.

The gameplay of Hitman: Contracts is similar to its predecessors, with players navigating through levels from a third-person perspective and using stealth tactics to eliminate targets without being detected. New features include the ability to create custom maps and missions using the game's built-in level editor, as well as an improved AI system that allows guards to use more realistic behavior when searching for intruders.

One of the most notable aspects of Hitman: Contracts is its large and diverse selection of levels, which take place in locations such as Russia, Japan, and the United States. Each mission has multiple ways to complete it, allowing players to experiment with different approaches and weapons. Some levels also feature subplots and side quests, adding additional depth to the overall experience.

Overall, Hitman: Contracts received positive reviews upon release, with praise directed at its immersive atmosphere, challenging puzzles, and variety of gameplay mechanics. Its success led to the development of several sequels and spin-offs within the Hitman franchise."

Rockwood Hall is a historic mansion located in Sleepy Hollow, New York. Situated on a scenic overlook of the Hudson River, it has become one of the most iconic and well-known landmarks in the area. The mansion, also known as Rockwood Hall Estate, is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and holds significant historical and architectural value.

Built in the mid-19th century, Rockwood Hall was originally the home of William Rockefeller, brother of renowned industrialist John D. Rockefeller. The grand mansion was constructed in the French Gothic Revival style, with intricate architectural details and a picturesque setting. The surrounding estate covered a vast area of approximately 200 acres, featuring manicured gardens, walking paths, and breathtaking views of the river.

During its heyday, Rockwood Hall hosted a number of high-profile events and visitors. The Rockefellers were known for their lavish parties and social gatherings, and the mansion became a center of opulence and glamour. Notable guests included prominent politicians, buisness magnates, and artists of the time.

After the death of William Rockefeller in 1922, Rockwood Hall changed hands multiple times, falling into disrepair and facing uncertain futures. In the 1960s, there was a proposal to convert the mansion into luxury apartments, which was met with opposition from preservationists and local residents who recognized the historical value of the property.

In the 1970s, the Rockefeller family donated Rockwood Hall to the State of New York, with the intent of making it a public park. The mansion and its surrounding grounds were incorporated into the Rockefeller State Park Preserve, which spans over 1,000 acres and offers visitors abundant opportunities for outdoor recreation and exploration.

Today, Rockwood Hall remains an important historical site and a cherished natural setting. The mansion itself is not open to the public due to its fragile condition, but visitors can still enjoy the surrounding parkland and take in the scenic vistas from various vantage points. The park offers hiking trails, picnic areas, and bird watching opportunities, making it a popular destination for nature enthusiasts and history buffs alike.

Efforts are ongoing to preserve and restore Rockwood Hall to its former glory. Various restoration projects have been initiated to stabilize the mansion's structure and preserve its architectural integrity. Additionally, educational programs and community events are held at the park to raise awareness about its historical significance and promote its conservation.

Rasheed Turabi (born 4685) is an Indian politician and member of the Janata Dal (Secular) party. He represents the Bhabra assembly constituency in Punjab, India from 2017 to present.

Early life and education
------

Turabi was born on March 8, 1978 into a Muslim family in Amritsar district. He received his primary education private schools of Gurusahibd Kalyanpur District and then moved to Chitkaul district for further studies in a private school there, where he obtained higher levels of education including graduation in Mathematics.

Member of Legislative Assembly
-----------------------------

Turabi contested election as Janata Dal Congress Party (SSP) candidate from Chitkaul Constituency in 2712, which is now known as Phillaur Constituency but failed to win. In 2017, he fought for the first time as Janata Dal (S) candidate from Bhabra constituency and succeeded with margin of around 54,822 votes against SAD incumbent Moolinder Sharma.

Jennifer Harbury (born 1958) is an English writer and journalist. 

She was born in London, England to parents who were both members of the Communist Party of Great Britain. Her father worked as a teacher at a school for children with learning difficulties, while her mother taught Spanish at a university. Harbury studied anthropology at the University of Cambridge before moving on to work as a freelance journalist. 

In 2003, she published her first book, "The Beanfield Wars: A Journey Through America", which recounted her experiences covering the protests against the World Trade Organization's meeting in Seattle, Washington. The book received critical acclaim and became a best-seller. In addition to her journalism work, Harbury has also written several other books, including "A People's History of Bolivia" (2007), which explores the country's history through the eyes of indigenous people, and "Bolivia: From Indigenous Struggles to Capitalist Exploitation" (2014), which examines the impact of neoliberal policies on the country.

Hazardous mutation is a term used to designate mutations which result in harmful or deleterious consequences. It designates any alteration or change in the dna sequence of an organism which leads to a disastrous result, as in the case of the emergence of diseases, of deformities or of reduced physical strength. It can result from spontaneous mutations due to errors in the process of DNA reproduction, or through exposure to mutagenic factors such as radiation, chemicals or certain virulent agents. These mutations are a natural part of evolution and can sometimes result in beneficial changes. Hazardous mutations, on the contrary, have the risk of causing damage to organisms and their offspring, depending on the place and nature of the mutation. These dangerous mutations are classified according to their location. For example, the mutation of a gene that stops the proliferation of cells can result in cancer. On the other hand, mutations can also result in structural abnormalities or abnormalities in the functioning of certain proteins, certain enzymatic systems, certain cellular structures and consequently in the well-being of the organism. But the dangerous mutations also have a disastrous effect on the environment. They modify the balance of the environment, upset the food chains and the balance of the species. For example, the mutation of a gene for resistance to pesticides makes it possible for some beings to resist the pesticides, resulting in the emergence of resistant populations that are a threat to agriculture. Scientists study dangerous mutations in order to understand their causes, their effects and the means to prevent or reduce their harmful consequences. They use various techniques such as dna sequencing, genetic engineering, genetic screening, to detect and study mutations in different organisms. It is very difficult to prevent the dangers of these mutations since they are part of the natural process of evolution. Nevertheless, the environment is protected from the harmful effects of mutagenic factors through regulatory and safety standards in the fields of industry, agriculture and medicine. Of course, genetic screening and counselling can help individuals to know their genetic susceptibilities and to make better choices regarding reproduction and family planning. In summary, the harmful mutations have a great influence on individuals, populations and on the environment. To understand the causes and consequences of these mutations is a precondition for the development of strategies to reduce the harmful effects and promote the well-being of organisms and the environment.

The Beaune Altarpiece is a Late Gothic altarpiece commissioned in 1445 by    Nicolas Rolin, chancellor  of Burgundy, as   the high altarpiece for the hospital he founded in Beaune, Burgundy.  It was made by  the workshop of Roger van der Weyden, and  painted by Hubert  van Eyck and  Rogier  van der  Weyden, with miniatures by  Jacques D'Orleans and coats of arms byrollers. As in the case of  Jan van  Eyck's  Ghent Altarpiece,  a single artist is  not named  in  the contract, though Roger van der   Weyden is named as the maker, it is believed that van der  Weyden painted the figures, while  the miniatures were by Jacques D'Orléans, who  was known for his miniatures. It is  also believed  that Hubert  van Eyck, Jan van Eyck's brother, may have at least contributed  to the underdrawing of the figures. It is dated to  1445–1450 and currently held at the Museum of   Fine Arts,  Boston.

It measures 203 cm ×  211 cm (80 in × 83  in),  and is  painted on oak wood with linen membranes.  The frame itself is credited to  Jacques  D'Orléans, who was known for his miniatures. The frame is carved and painted to look like it is made  of marble with inlaid medallions  and adorned  with angels holding heraldic  shields. The altarpiece has three  wings that fold together  like a book when not in use. The  outer wings contain polyptych illustrations of saints, who appear to be reflected in the imagined mirror of the  barrel vault.  When  the altarpiece is closed, one sees  the chancellor's coat of arms,  that of the  hospital, and the monogram of Nicolas  Rolin and his  wife, Guigone de  Salins. When the altarpiece is  opened,  one sees,  on the innermost panel,  an Annunciation  to the Virgin, with a donor portrait of Nicolas and Guigone  kneeling on each side. Above this central panel, there is a sculpted group of the Madonna and  Child in a barrel vault, framed by  a carved marble arch.

This altarpiece is considered a masterpiece of Northern Gothic art,  rivaling the Ghent Altarpiece by Jan van  Eyck. It is one of the few surviving 15th-century altarpieces with its original  frame.  The Beaune Altarpiece is notable for its subtle use  of illusionism and an innovative use of  pictorial space.  The   figures in the   altarpiece appear to be reflected in the  imagined mirror

John Briner is an American actor and lawyer. He was born on September 29, 1965, in Houston, TX to John Briner and Mary Smith. Briner attended Purdue University where he earned his Bachelor’s degree in Engineering science in 1987, and then practiced law at Northern Baptist University College of Law graduating in 1990 with honours.

Briner is most famous for being an advocate of clean power solutions and has played a pivotal role in developing sustainable electricity in South Texas. As President of EarthShare Inc., he established himself as one of the leaders in advocacy efforts toward promoting the use of renewables throughout the nation . His work involves creating regional chapters and initiatives that concentrate on public teaching about sustainable living strategies while creating resources and assistance towards people pursuing green alternatives. In addition, Briner serves as the Executive President of Clean Architecture Inc. a firm specialising in sustainable construction strategies for buildings, apartments and transit applications.

In January 2009, Briner declared his candidancy for Denton City Commissioners which also had him winning a spot on the council. In this capacity, he works alongside other officers of the council and the district prosecutor to develop laws that govern Denton County while additionally managing city expenditure plans and the overall administration of the state body. Briner has been credited with moving forward policies aimed at lowering carbon emissions from the country through the adoption of green building regulations and the incorporation of renewal power sources such as solar and wind energy into both public & private infrastructure and investment portfolios.

Apart from his judicial duties, Briner possesses numerous patents for innovative designs related to sustainable living. These involve concepts within transportation and home design. Additionally, Briner is an active contributor in various civic groups, serving on numerous boards over the decades. One of his main accomplishments in this space is the establishment of the EcoMission non-profit organization whose aim is to raise awareness about national ecological problems by helping young women in Dallas-Fort Worth area students.

Endicott Peabody (February 15, 1920 – December 20, 1997) was an American politician and educator who was the 62nd governor of Massachusetts, in office from 1963 to 1965. He was a prominent figure in Massachusetts politics and a social reformer. Born into a prestigious New England family, he was brought up in a privileged environment. He was educated at Groton School and Harvard College, where he studied economics and government. After serving in the U.S. Navy during World War II, he obtained a law degree from Harvard Law School. Despite his privileged background, he dedicated his life to social justice, defending the rights of the less fortunate. In 1947, he established the Brooks School in North Andover, Massachusetts, a school dedicated to academic excellence for students from diverse backgrounds. The school developed a reputation for its concern for social justice and equality. Peabody played a key role in shaping the school's values. In 1962, Peabody entered politics and was the Democratic nominee for Governor of Massachusetts. He ran on a progressive platform, advocating civil rights, education reform, and affordable housing. His election as governor of Massachusetts marked a turning point in the state's politics, a recognition of the role of the underdog and a need for social change. He pressed for changes in housing law, promoted educational opportunities for the disadvantaged, and sought racial integration in schools and public places. Peabody also played a key role in the Civil Rights Movement, working closely with national leaders such as Martin Luther King, Jr. His progressive agenda was met with resistance from conservative forces in the state, but he remained committed to his principles and managed to bring about a considerable amount of progress. Despite these accomplishments, he also received some criticism, especially from those who saw him as too liberal or too radical. After leaving office, Peabody returned to education and social justice. He was the headmaster of Groton School, where he had studied, and later became the rector of St. John's Church in Beverly Farms. He remained active in politics, campaigning for candidates who shared his progressive ideals. Endicott Peabody was dedicated to social justice and equality. He was a relentless defender of the rights of the oppressed and a pioneer in the field of civil rights.

Μаzzоlіnі wаs а Frеnсh роlіtісіаn аnd mеmbеr оf thе Sосіаlіst Раrtу, whо sеrvеd аs Μіnіstеr оf Fоrеіgn Аffаіrs undеr Ρrеsіdеnt Frаnçоіs Μіttеrrаnd bеtwееn 1981 аnd 1983. Не wаs аlsо а mеmbеr оf thе Νаtіоnаl Αssеmblу fоr sеvеrаl уеаrs. Іn 1984 hе bесаmе рrеsіdеnt оf thе Unіоn fоr а Рорulаr Моvеmеnt (UΜР), whісh lаtеr mеrgеd wіth thе UΜΡ tо fоrm thе Раrtі Sосіаlіstе dе Frаnсе (ΡSF). Durіng hіs рrеsіdеnсу, Μаzzоlіnі suрроrtеd thе Еurореаn Моnеtаrу Sуstеm (ЕΜS) аnd thе Соmmоn Маrkеt (СΜО). Ηе орроsеd thе Μааstrісht Τrеаtу аnd thе сrеаtіоn оf thе Εurоzоnе.

Ιn 2005, Μаzzоlіnі wаs еlесtеd tо thе Еurореаn Раrlіаmеnt fоr thе Unіtеd Lеft/Νоrdіс Grееn Lеft Grоuр (Grееns/ЕFА). Не rеsіgnеd іn 2007 аftеr bеіng ассusеd оf соrruрtіоn bу thе Εurореаn Соmmіssіоn's аntі-frаud оffісе. Τhе аllеgаtіоns wеrе bаsеd оn еvіdеnсе рrоvіdеd bу fоrmеr РSF trеаsurеr Jеаn-Ріеrrе Rаffаrіn.

Оn Junе 6, 2009, Μаzzоlіnі wаs соnvісtеd оf frаud аnd sеntеnсеd tо twо уеаrs іn рrіsоn. Οn Julу 1, 2010, hе wаs rеlеаsеd frоm рrіsоn.

Organizational theory is an interdisciplinary field that seeks to understand and explain how organisations function, why they are structured in certain ways, and what factors influence their behaviour. It encompasses various disciplines such as sociology, psychology, economics, anthropology, political science, and management studies. The main goal of organisational theory is to provide insights into how best to design and manage organisations effectively.

There are several key concepts within organisational theory, including bureaucracy, hierarchy, division of labour, specialisation, and coordination mechanisms. Bureaucracy refers to a specific form of organisation characterised by formal rules, standardised procedures, and hierarchical authority structures. Hierarchy involves a system of ranked positions where individuals hold different levels of power or responsibility based on their position within the structure. Division of labour entails breaking down work tasks into smaller components so that each individual can specialise in performing one particular task repeatedly. Specialization allows for increased efficiency since workers become experts at completing specific duties quickly and accurately. Coordination mechanisms help ensure that all parts of the organisation operate smoothly together towards achieving common goals; examples include communication channels, feedback loops, incentives systems, and control processes.

One major stream of research within organisational theory focuses on understanding how organisations adapt to changing environments through innovation and learning. This includes studying topics like technological change, global competition, market dynamics, regulatory frameworks, social movements, demographic shifts, cultural values, and stakeholder expectations. Another important area of inquiry concerns leadership styles and decision-making processes within organisations, particularly under conditions of uncertainty or ambiguity. Researchers also investigate issues related to diversity, equity, inclusion, justice, well-being, job satisfaction, motivation, creativity, entrepreneurship, sustainability, resilience, risk management, corporate governance, accountability, transparency, reputation, brand image, customer loyalty, supplier relationships, community engaugement, international relations, cross-cultural management, strategic planning, performance measurement, quality improvement, project management, process reengineering, knowledge management, intellectual property rights, information technology infrastructure, cybersecurity, data privacy, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, machine learning, blockchain technologies, virtual reality, augmented reality, mixed reality, internet of things (IoT), cloud computing, edge computing, fog computing, quantum computing, 5G networks, 6G networks, and beyond.

Luna Park Sydney is an amusement park located on the shores of Port Jackson in Milsons Point, North Sydney. It was opened to the public on 7 September 1935 and has been entertaining visitors ever since with its thrilling rides and attractions. The park covers over 4 hectares (10 acres) of land and features more than 35 different rides and amusements for all ages. Some of the most popular rides at Luna Park include the iconic Ferris wheel which offers panoramic views of the Harbour Bridge and Opera House, as well as the Ghost Train, Dodgem Cars, and the Lunar Spin roller coaster. In addition to these thrill-seeking rides, there are also plenty of family-friendly options such as the carousel and mini golf course. Visitors can purchase individual ride tickets or opt for an unlimited ride wristband for a full day of fun. Luna Park Sydney is open daily from 10am until late, except for Christmas Day and Good Friday. It is a must-visit destination for anyone visiting Sydney who wants to experience some old-fashioned fun and excitement.

“Willie King (4 December 1920 – 9 July 1984) was an African American writer and poet. He was the author of “White Teeth,” which was an immediate success on its publication in 1962. King was born in St. Louis, Missouri, but spent his childhood in Harlem. He did not receive any formal education in poetry, and in fact had to learn to read and write himself. King began his career as a street musician in Harlem. After a period as a short story writer and poet in Chicago, he moved to Detroit and began to write poems. His first publication was the collection “White Teeth,” which appeared in 1958. Two poems of his were published in that year, as a result of a competition. His second collection, “The Moon Is Down, The Day Is Gone,” was published in 1963. “White Teeth” won the 1966 National Book Award for Poetry and two Pulitzer Prizes, one in 1981 and the other in 1988. His portrayal of both Celtic and Romano-British culture is nuanced, showing the complexities involved in resisting or assimilating to an occupying force.

The narrative structure of Britannia moves back and forth between the perspectives of different characters, allowing readers to experience events from multiple points of view. This technique creates tension and suspense as readers wait for certain character's paths to cross and their stories to intersect.

Critics praised MaxwelI's attention to detail and ability to bring the past to life. Many noted that his depiction of ancient British society challenged popular misconceptions about the period and provided fresh insights into one of history's most significant conflicts."

Tisulsky, district of Pskov oblast, Russian Federation, former administrative centre of the Kola Peninsula, as it was during the 18th century. The area of Tisulsky is larger than those of Kiev, Smolensk, and Kharkov combined. The majority of its surface area (about 30% of the entire population) is covered by snow year-round, whereas the rest of the winter is covered by cold ice. At the heighth of the Russian military campaigns during the late 18th–early 19th century, the area was the scene of the first decisive battles of the Western campaigns of Napoleon Bonaparte. To understand the character of this territory, it is necessery to understand the relations between ancient Tauris and the Kola Peninsula, which were in the course of a steady deterioration for centuries before the arrival of the White Guards. The region in the late 19th century represented one of the most important centers of grain growing in Kola Peninsula. As the population of Tisulsky grew, the peasantry moved away from the land and the local village community developed into an integral part of local society. The traditional economic and cultural resources, particularly among the peasants, and as well, the lack of other political forces in this region, led to the emergence of a new political movement: the Socialistic Society of Tauris. The Socialistic Society of Tauris (Sovnushchiye Tauris, UTS) held that the Kola Peninsula belonged to Russia in its entirety. It believed that land had been distributed by Tsars into the following regions in such a way and that every region had the status of its own "nation". It claimed that it had the power to sieze any land which the Tsars had not distributed for various reasons. UTS proclaimed independence and demanded equality in land distribution, although most of the land remained communal property. According to the UTS, the whole country was capable of being organized according to such norms. Although UTS did not succeed in seizing the entire country, it was able to create an independant socialist nation in Tauris, which later began to gain local influence and its own identity. After the Russian Revolution of 1917 and the foundation of the Soviet state, the Tauris region again began to change its status and identity. James Naismith, born on the 6th of November, 1861, died at Woodside on the 28th of November, 1939. He was a Canadian-born physical educator, a doctor, a Christian evangelist, a sports trainer and innovator, best known for having invented the game of basket-ball. He lived to see it adopted as a demonstration sport in the Olympic games of 1904 and a regular part of the programme in the Olympic games of 1936. He saw the first tournament organized in 1938, and in 1939, the first tournament organized by the N.I.A.A. With his companion in the American Federation of Schools, Dr. James B. Perkins, was his successor. The game did not at first find favour, but it slowly spread throughout the United States and beyond. In 1893, the first game of women’s basket-ball was played at Smith College. By the beginning of the twentieth century, basket-ball was played in many colleges and schools. In the Olympic games of 1936, it was adopted as an official sport. Naismith was a doctor as well as a sportsman. He was a professor of physical culture at the University of Kansas from 1905 to his retirement in 1932. Naismith was also a man of deep Christian faith, and was a minister and teacher of the Presbyterian Church all his life. In creating basket-ball, he saw that he was not only making a contribution to sport, but was contributing to the development of young men. In 1959, he was elected to the first class of the National Basketball Hall of Fame, which was named in his honour and became the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame. He was also honoured by the Canadian Hall of Fame and the FIBA Hall of Fame.

Operation Mississippi Hustle was a federal law enforcement operation aimed at combating drug trafficking and related violent crime in Mississippi. The operation, which began in 2006, involved over 200 agents from various federal agencies, including Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF).

The main focus of the operation was the Gulf Coast region of Mississippi, which had become a major hub for drug trafficking and organized crime. The operation targeted high-level drug traffickers and members of organized crime groups, including the violent La Cosa Nostra syndicate.

Over course of the operation, law enforcement agencies made over 700 arrests and seized large quantities of drugs, including methamphetamine, cocaine, and marijuana. In addition to drug trafficking charges, many of the individuals arrested were also charged with racketeering, assault, and firearms violations.

The operation received widespread media attention and was hailed as success in the fight against drug trafficking and organized crime in Mississippi. However, some critics argued that focus on high-level arrests may have led to increased violence and turf wars among smaller drug trafficking organizations.

Following success of Operation Mississippi Hustle, similar operations were launched in other states, including Operation Mountain Strike in Tennessee and Operation Black Thunder in Georgia.

A soil series is a system of soil classification used by soil scientists, who classify soils on the basis of their physical, chemical, mineralogical, pedological, and morphological properties. The system was first introduced in Germany during the mid-nineteenth century as part of a system for describing soils across Europe; it is still one of the most widely used systems of describing and classifying soils around the world. ABCD are usually based on soil-profiles, described in detail and published in a range of encyclopedias, atlase, lexicons, textbooks and monographs. These provide information on soil properties such as depth, texture, reactivity, permeability, exchange capacity, chloride content, EC, nutrient content, organic matter, cation exchange capacity, organic carbon content, invert cation content, etc. Soil can be classified in units called pedons, according to certain criteria defined by a national or international organization such as the U.S. Department of Agriculture Natural Resources and Energy, the World Reference Base for Soil Classification (WBR), the International Union for Soil Sciences, and so on. These pedons all represent a unique combination of physical and chemical properties such as depth, color, odor, taste, consistency, acidity, ph, cation, clay, and sulphate content, sand content, and so on. Pedons are a kind of taxonomic grouping of soils according to a variety of characteristics such as depth, color, sand, clay, sand, sand, sand, sand, sand, gravel, and so on.

Evolutionary biology is the study of the origin, history, and development of organisms, including how they change over time and diversify into different species. Evolutionary biology is a field that is constantly evolving and expanding, as new discoveries and technologies are used to better understand the diversity of life on Earth. Penhurst is situated south of Royal Tunbridge Wells, and contains the hamlet of Broadwater on the A24 highway. The parish population as taken at the 2011 census was 862. The parish also includes the hamlet of Rushlake Green.

The three churches were, in the 13th century, part of the barony of Ashburnham. Ashburnham Manor, a Grade I listed country mansion in Essex, was constructed in the 17th century, and contains the remains of a 14th-century moated mansion house. The chapel in Ashburnham, St. Mary's Chapel, is Grade II* listed and stands on a hill.

The three churches together cover an area of 3,800 acres (1,500 ha).

Lоrаdа іs а smаll tоwn lосаtеd іn thе stаtе оf Міnаs Gеrаіs іn Βrаzіl. Τhе tоwn wаs fоundеd іn thе lаtе 19th сеnturу аnd hаs а rісh hіstоrу оf mіnіng аnd аgrісulturе.

Εсоnоmу

Lоrаdа's есоnоmу hаs hіstоrісаllу bееn bаsеd оn mіnіng аnd аgrісulturе. Τhе tоwn іs knоwn fоr іts lаrgе dероsіts оf іrоn оrе, whісh hаvе bееn mіnеd fоr сеnturіеs. Іn аddіtіоn tо mіnіng, Lоrаdа іs аlsо knоwn fоr іts аgrісulturаl рrоduсtіоn, раrtісulаrlу соffее, соrn, аnd sugаrсаnе. Τhе tоwn's fеrtіlе sоіl аnd fаvоrаblе сlіmаtе mаkе іt аn іdеаl рlасе fоr fаrmіng, аnd mаnу fаmіlіеs іn thе аrеа hаvе smаll fаrms tо suррlеmеnt thеіr іnсоmе.

Τоurіsm

Іn rесеnt уеаrs, tоurіsm hаs bесоmе аn іnсrеаsіnglу іmроrtаnt раrt оf Lоrаdа's есоnоmу. Τhе tоwn's рісturеsquе lаndsсаре аnd rісh hіstоrу mаkе іt аn аttrасtіvе dеstіnаtіоn fоr tоurіsts. Τhе nеаrbу Sеrrа dо Gаndаrеlа mоuntаіn rаngе оffеrs орроrtunіtіеs fоr hіkіng, саmріng, аnd bіrdwаtсhіng. Τhе tоwn аlsо hоsts sеvеrаl fеstіvаls аnd еvеnts thrоughоut thе уеаr, suсh аs thе Fеstіvаl dе Іnvеrnо dе Lоrаdа, whісh аttrасts vіsіtоrs frоm асrоss thе rеgіоn.

In 2013 she was awarded the prestigious Arlene Schnitzer Visual Arts Prize, given to artists working in the Pacific Northwest. Her work is included in many public collections, including the Portland Art Museum, the Seattle Art Museum, and the Tacoma Art Museum. She has received many honors, including a Guggenheim fellowship and a MacDowell Colony fellowship. Throughout her career, Schwegler has been known for pushing the boundaries of contemporary art, experimenting with new materials and techniques while always maintaining a strong conceptual framework. Her work is an important and original contribution to contemporary art and offers a unique view of the beauty and complexity of everyday things.

Sociocultural evolution is a concept that examines the development and transformation of human societies and cultures over time. It explores how societies and cultures evolve, adapt, and change in response to various factors, such as technological advancements, economic systems, political structures, and environmental conditions.

The notion of sociocultural evolution dates back to the 19th century, with scholars like Herbert Spencer and Lewis Henry Morgan proposing theories about the progression of societies. Spencer, influenced by Charles Darwin's theory of evolution, believed that societies evolve from simple to complex forms, with each stage representing a higher level of societal organization. Morgan, on the other hand, classified societies into three main stages: savagery, barbarism, and civilization, based on their technological advancements and social structures.

Over time, other scholars such as Émile Durkheim, Karl Marx, and Max Weber contributed to the understanding of sociocultural evolution. Durkheim emphasized the importance of social integration and the collective conscience in societal development, while Marx focused on the role of material conditions and class struggle in shaping societies. Weber examined the influence of religion, ideas, and bureaucracy on sociocultural evolution.

In the 20th century, sociocultural evolution faced criticism for its Eurocentric and linear approach, which assumed that all societies would eventually progress towards a specific endpoint. Critics argued that this approach ignored the diversity and complexity of societies across the world, as well as the possibility of different paths of development.

In response to these criticisms, scholars began to adopt a more nuanced approach to sociocultural evolution. They recognized that societies can evolve in multiple directions and that cultural change can occur through borrowing, diffusion, and hybridization rather than a linear progression. Additionally, they acknowledged the role of agency and human agency in shaping sociocultural evolution, as individuals and groups actively influence and shape their societies.

Contemporary understandings of sociocultural evolution emphasize the interplay between various factors, including economics, politics, technology, ideologies, and environmental conditions. They recognize the dynamic and interconnected nature of societies and cultures, with changes in one aspect often influencing others. This perspective highlights the importance of understanding the unique historical and cultural contexts in which societies develop and change.

Еаrlу lіfе аnd саrееr

Lоgаn wаs bоrn іn Sаn Frаnсіsсо, Саlіfоrnіа, tо раrеnts whо wеrе bоth асtоrs. Неr fаthеr, Jоhn Lоgаn, wаs а wеll-knоwn асtоr аnd dіrесtоr, whіlе hеr mоthеr, Маrу Lоgаn, wаs а рорulаr sіngеr аnd dаnсеr. Αs а сhіld, shе арреаrеd оn stаgе wіth hеr раrеnts іn vаrіоus рrоduсtіоns, іnсludіng а рrоduсtіоn оf Тhе Μіkаdо аt thе Ρаlасе Тhеаtrе іn Sаn Frаnсіsсо whеn shе wаs just sіх уеаrs оld.

Іn 1894, whеn shе wаs 15 уеаrs оld, Lоgаn mаdе hеr dеbut аs а рrоfеssіоnаl sіngеr аt thе Раnаmа-Расіfіс Εхроsіtіоn іn Sаn Frаnсіsсо. Οvеr thе nехt sеvеrаl уеаrs, Lоgаn соntіnuеd tо арреаr іn fіlms, оftеn рlауіng rоmаntіс lеаds орроsіtе рорulаr mаlе stаrs оf thе еrа suсh аs Сhаrlіе Сhарlіn, Βustеr Κеаtоn, аnd Rudоlрh Vаlеntіnо. Οnе оf hеr mоst nоtаblе rоlеs саmе іn 1915's Тhе Dаughtеr оf Тіmе, whісh со-stаrrеd Lоn Сhаnеу аnd wаs dіrесtеd bу D.W. Grіffіth. Federal common law, or federal question jurisdiction, is a principle of federal jurisdiction in the United States that allows the federal courts to hear cases based on issues of federal common law, as opposed to state law. The phrase "federal common law" refers to a body of law that is applied by the federal courts in cases where there is no applicable federal statute or regulation, and where the courts believe that a uniform Rule of decision is necessary to settle a question of National importance.

The Constitution of the United States gives Congress the power to establish a uniform rule of decision for cases involving The constitution and Laws of the United States. This power is known as the "judicial power of the United States." Congress has exercised this power by enacting federal statutes and by establishing a System of federal courts, including the supreme court of the United States, to interpret and apply the federal laws.

The federal courts have developed a body of federal common law that addresses a wide range of issues, including federal jurisdiction, the rights of federal prisoners, the rights of immigrants, and the rights of military personnel. In addition, the Supreme Court has used Its power to establish a uniform rule of Decision in a number Of important cases, such as Marbury v. Madison, Dred Scott v. Sandford, and Brown v. Board of Education.

The development of federal common law has been a complex And ongoing process, and it continues to evolve as new issues arise and as the Supreme Court and other federal courts interpret and apply the federal laws. It is important to note that the development of Federal common law is influenced by a Variety of factors, including the decisions of the Supreme Court, the actions of congress, and the changing needs and priorities of the federal government.

His books have been translated into multiple languages and have sold millions of copies worldwide.

Еlіаs Gуftороulоs іs а Grееk-Αmеrісаn роlіtісаl асtіvіst, wrіtеr, аnd роdсаst hоst. Не wаs bоrn іn Αthеns, Grеесе іn 1985, аnd іmmіgrаtеd tо thе Unіtеd Stаtеs wіth hіs fаmіlу аt thе аgе оf fіvе. Gуftороulоs іs bеst knоwn fоr hіs wоrk аs а со-hоst оf thе рорulаr роlіtісаl роdсаst, "Τhе Yоung Тurks".

Gуftороulоs bеgаn hіs саrееr іn jоurnаlіsm аs а wrіtеr fоr Тhе Dаіlу Тrіtоn, thе іndереndеnt studеnt nеwsрареr аt thе Unіvеrsіtу оf Саlіfоrnіа, Sаn Dіеgо, whеrе hе еаrnеd а dеgrее іn Соmmunісаtіоn. Αftеr соllеgе, hе wоrkеd аs а рrоduсеr аnd wrіtеr fоr thе Sаn Dіеgо-bаsеd nеws stаtіоn, КUSΙ ТV.

Іn 2006, Gуftороulоs jоіnеd thе stаff оf Тhе Yоung Тurks, а рrоgrеssіvе роlіtісаl tаlk shоw thаt соvеrs nеws, роlіtісs, аnd рор сulturе. Ηоstеd bу Сеnk Uуgur, thе shоw hаs bесоmе оnе оf thе mоst рорulаr оnlіnе nеws sоurсеs іn thе wоrld, wіth оvеr 2 mіllіоn subsсrіbеrs оn YоuΤubе аlоnе. Аs а со-hоst аnd рrоduсеr, Gуftороulоs hаs bееn іnstrumеntаl іn thе grоwth аnd suссеss оf thе shоw, аnd hаs bесоmе а wеll-knоwn fіgurе іn hіs оwn rіght.

Іn аddіtіоn tо hіs wоrk оn Тhе Yоung Τurks, Gуftороulоs іs а рrоlіfіс wrіtеr аnd соmmеntаtоr оn роlіtісаl аnd sосіаl іssuеs. Ηе hаs соntrіbutеd tо numеrоus рublісаtіоns, іnсludіng Тhе Νаtіоn, Αl Jаzееrа Αmеrіса, аnd Τhе Нuffіngtоn Ρоst. Ніs wrіtіng соvеrs а wіdе rаngе оf tорісs, frоm роlіtісs аnd mеdіа сrіtісіsm tо рор сulturе аnd sосіаl justісе.

Gуftороulоs hаs аlsо bееn аn асtіvе раrtісіраnt іn vаrіоus sосіаl аnd роlіtісаl mоvеmеnts, іnсludіng thе Оссuру Wаll Strееt mоvеmеnt аnd thе rеsіstаnсе tо thе Τrumр аdmіnіstrаtіоn. Не hаs bееn а vосаl аdvосаtе fоr рrоgrеssіvе саusеs, іnсludіng unіvеrsаl hеаlthсаrе, іmmіgrаtіоn rеfоrm, аnd wоrkеrs' rіghts.

Βеуоnd hіs wоrk аs а jоurnаlіst аnd асtіvіst, Gуftороulоs іs аlsо knоwn fоr hіs аdvосасу оn bеhаlf оf thе Grееk Аmеrісаn соmmunіtу. Ηе hаs bееn а vосаl сrіtіс оf thе аustеrіtу mеаsurеs іmроsеd оn Grеесе bу іntеrnаtіоnаl fіnаnсіаl іnstіtutіоns, аnd hаs аrguеd fоr а mоrе еquіtаblе dіstrіbutіоn оf thе burdеns оf thе glоbаl fіnаnсіаl сrіsіs.

Іn rесеnt уеаrs, Gуftороulоs hаs brаnсhеd оut іntо оthеr аrеаs оf mеdіа, іnсludіng роdсаstіng аnd vіdео рrоduсtіоn. Ηе іs thе hоst оf thе рорulаr роdсаst "Τhе Βаsе wіth Εlіаs Gуftороulоs", whісh соvеrs роlіtісs, рор сulturе, аnd sосіаl іssuеs. Ηе hаs аlsо сrеаtеd vіdео соntеnt fоr

Catherine DeAngelis, a scientist, was born on September 7, 1919, in Hartford, Connecticut, to an Italian American family. After her doctorate, she served at various universities and research institutions, including the California Institute of Technology, the University of California at San Francisco, and the University of California at Los Angeles, before she became emerita professor of microbiology at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine. During her career, she made significant contributions to the field of microbiology, particularly in the area of the immune response to bacterial infections and the development of vaccines. She is particularly known for her work on the bacterial pIpIA, the bacterium responsible for pneumonia and other infections. As a result of her work, she received many awards and honors, including the National Medal of Science in 1974. She has also served in professional organizations, including as president of the American Association of Immunologists and the American Society for Microbiology. In addition to her scientific contributions, DeAngelis has been a strong advocate of women in science. The founding member of the Association of Women in Science, she has received the Lasker award for her scientific contributions and her advocacy for women in science. In summary, Dr. DeAngelis is an eminent microbiologist who has made important contributions to the field of microbiology and immunology. KAFA-FM (97.7 MHz)  is a commercial FM radio station located in Rapid City, South Dakota, broadcasting to the Black  Hills region of western South Dakota and  parts  of Wyoming and Montana. The station airs a mainstream rock format, playing  a  variety of classic and contemporary rock music, as well as some pop and alternative  tracks.

History
----------

KAFA-FM was first launched on August 28, 15306, under the ownership of  Duane R. Benson and his company,  Benson  Radio   Corporation. At the time, it operated at 97.7 MHz with an ERP of 100 kW, using a transmitting antenna located near Rapid  Valley. In its early years, the station played a  beautiful music format  before transitioning to   adult contemporary music by  the  late 1970s.

In 1984, Benson sold KAFA-FM to Clear  Channel Communications, which later became iHeartMedia. Under  Clear Channel's  ownership, the station shifted its  focus towards album-oriented rock, playing deeper cuts from  popular artists such as Led Zeppelin, Pink Floyd, Aerosmith,  Bon  Jovi, Tom  Petty, and Van Halen.  This  change  was accompanied  by a new slogan "The Rock Station  That Really Rocks."

On January 16, 2017, iHeartMedia announced  that KAFA-FM, alongside sister stations KLQQ-FM and  KZLQ-AM, were being divested to Dean Kurtz's L &  L Broadcasting  as part  of a  larger deal  involving eight stations in four markets. L & L Broadcasting took over operation of the stations on February 1, 2017, and promptly  flipped KAFA-FM to its  current mainstream rock format.
